newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's "dirty old car" breaks down in space.
newsitem.headline: Russia's "dirty old car" breaks down in space.

text.p: Stumbling around in the sticky darkness on the Mir space station, the cosmonauts aboard the world's only orbital laboratory can have little sense of being at the cutting edge of mankind's probing of the cosmos.

"A very dirty and grimy camping trip in an old car" was how NASA physicist Michael Foale described life on Mir -- and that was before the latest emergency on Thursday that forced him and his two Russian colleagues to shut off most of their life-support systems and turn out the lights.

Foale, 40, also compared the lack of home comforts to life at his English boarding school. But even the phlegmatic American must be feeling the tension aboard the stricken ship as he gropes his way round by torchlight, trying to patch things up. It is a long way from sneaking round the dorm for a midnight feast.

Mir was launched in 1986 as Russia was starting to open to the world and the Cold War space race was nearing its end. It has been built up into a 140-tonne complex of half a dozen mainly laboratory modules, in cooperation with NASA and European and other foreign space agencies.

It has provided a testbed for the international space station Alpha, now being developed, has offered a unique platform for scientific experiments that can only be performed in zero gravity, and generated vital foreign income for the Russian space industry after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

But it was only ever designed to fly for five years and the discomforts of months aboard are vivid in recollections of former crew members, despite their sense of privilege at working and living on mankind's only permanent home in the heavens.

After 11 years, the living quarters show signs of age. Cosmonauts complain of all-pervasive grubbiness -- despite the efforts of NASA's Shannon Lucid, who a Russian space official with no regard for political correctness said would bring a woman's touch with the duster during her stay on Mir last year.

The toilets nearly overflowed this year and it was the extra load of waste, some of it "organic", that according to unconfirmed reports contributed to the collision with an unmanned cargo craft on June 25, starting Mir's latest problems.

Foale spent an uncomfortable fortnight without a toothbrush after he lost his personal belongings in the punctured Spektr module. He got a new toilet kit aboard a relief freighter, but he and his colleagues still must repair cabling on Spektr.

The tension seems to have got the better of commander Vasily Tsibliyev, 43. Despite the plastic bunny lucky charm he carries from his daughter, Tsibliyev developed a heart flutter this week and Foale has been asked to step into a spacesuit to carry out the repairs with flight engineer, Alexander Lazutkin, 39.
Yet the latest problem may put those repairs off again.

It may have been stress and fatigue after three weeks in even darker, sweatier and less active conditions than usual that caused one of the three -- officials would not say who -- to pull out a wrong computer cable, plunging Mir into crisis on Thursday.

A loss of power threw its solar panels out of line with the Sun, forcing the crew to shut down non-vital systems in order to charge up batteries over long hours, or even days, so that they can eventually jump-start the gyroscopic guidance system.
Until then, they must breathe canned air -- they have five days' supply -- and bear temperatures and humidities that will be acceptable for up to three days but are no longer controlled.

There is little question of being rescued by some sort of galactic breakdown service, though a NASA Shuttle flight might be a remote possibility. But the spacemen can always fly home aboard their tiny Soyuz escape craft -- provided they do not burn up its fuel in trying to connect Mir's misalignment.
